newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Greenspan takes the spotlight.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Greenspan takes the spotlight.

text.p: U.S. credit markets will likely stay defensive on Wednesday as players tune in to Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's long-awaited Humphrey-Hawkins congressional testimony, analysts said.

"The market is nervous ahead of Greenspan's testimony ... and it's certainly defensive given all the back-up we've seen since Tuesday last week," said Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.

Greenspan will deliver the first leg of his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins address on Wednesday. The second part will take place on March 5. Wall Street analysts said the market will be all ears to the Fed chairman's words.
The speech gains even more importance now, when data stubbornly show the economy continues to grow at a fairly strong pace, labor markets remain tight but with no sign of inflationary pressures.
"The market is waiting for Greenspan to provide some light, some guidance to where we're going to go from here," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
So what is Greenspan expected to say?

"It seems the general feeling is that Greenspan's remarks won't be much different from what he's been saying all along -- that the Fed is going to be vigilant (against inflation) and the risks are on the upside," said Raphael Marrone, economist at Deustche Morgan Grenfell.

Experts said, however, Wall Street is a bit afraid the Fed chairman might suggest in any way that inflation might pick up somewhat in the months to come. "The market is worried about him making a loaded phrase about the inflation outlook. That could be treated negatively," Leahey said.
Analysts also said Greenspan was expected to express some concern about the possibility that higher equity prices may lead to a pick-up in consumer spending via a wealth effect.
The Fed chairman is also expected to drop a few words on the state of the country's monetary aggregates.
"The market will probably treat that as a negative because that's another way to talk about strength in the economy," Leahey said.
On the other hand, analysts said the market may put in a good performance on Wednesday if Greenspan says that inflation remains dormant for the time being.
Market participants will also take in some fresh supply on Wednesday after a frustating two-year note auction on Tuesday.
The Treasury will offer players $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday after placing some $17.5 billion in two-year notes at a 5.885 percent yield on Tuesday with a 2.21 bid-to-cover ratio.
Analysts said the auction performance, however, will depend on whether the market likes Greenspan's comments.
"It's going to be a Greenspan auction," Leahey said.
On Tuesday, the Federal Reserve added permanent reserves to the banking system through a coupon pass. The Fed bought coupons from May 15, 2002, to February 15, 2007, for delivery on Wednesday.
Analysts said federal funds were expected to open at 5.38 percent on Wednesday, above the Fed's 5.25 percent target for the rate.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was quoted down 1/32 at 99-18/32 in late Tuesday trade to yield 6.66 percent.
